strengths: Introduces a well-motivated formalization of payload recoverability along two complementary axes (tokens→buckets, buckets→secret), grounded in classifier-based steganalysis literature, which gives a principled way to compare steganographic schemes rather than relying on ad hoc distributional metrics.

The embedding-space hyperplane encoding/bucketing scheme is a conceptually elegant idea that ties the covert channel to the model's own learned geometry, and the paper empirically demonstrates it simultaneously improves exact-match accuracy and reduces recoverability across multiple models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B) and two datasets, which is a non-trivial joint result.

The theoretical KL-divergence and perplexity lower bounds (Theorems 7.1/7.2) provide a principled argument for why standard distributional steganalysis is fundamentally limited for fine-tuning-based attacks, adding rigor beyond purely empirical claims.

The mechanistic interpretability detection approach (linear probes on late-layer activations) is a novel and interesting defense angle, and the secret-conditioned XOR-masking control is a thoughtful ablation that convincingly decouples output-level recoverability from internal detectability, strengthening the paper's central claim that internal signatures persist even when output decoding is prevented.

Reasonably extensive experimental scope: full vs. LoRA fine-tuning, in-distribution and out-of-distribution prompt generalization, and multiple text-quality metrics (coherence, stability, perplexity, KL), with appendix details supporting reproducibility (hyperparameters, classifier configurations, probe protocols).
weaknesses: Despite the reported relative gains (+78-123%), absolute exact-match accuracies remain modest (roughly 19-43%), and results are inconsistent across settings (e.g., minimal or negative gains for Ministral-8B full fine-tuning, occasional underperformance cases), which tempers claims about the practical severity/generalizability of the improved attack.

The recoverability metric is instantiated with a specific, limited set of classifiers (XGBoost, MLP); the paper acknowledges but does not empirically test more sophisticated seed-recovery or cryptanalytic approaches an adversary might use, so the claimed reduction in recoverability could be optimistic.

The proposed mechanistic detection method assumes white-box access to hidden states, a strong assumption that the authors themselves flag as a limitation; no output-only or black-box detection baseline is evaluated, and there is no comparison against existing steganalysis detectors (e.g., classifier-based methods cited in related work) to contextualize how much of an advance the probing approach represents.

The theoretical bounds in Section 7 are derived under simplified assumptions (e.g., a specific peaked-distribution example, single hyperplane pooling) and are not directly validated against the empirical text-quality measurements in Section 6.4, which only use 1 bit/token; the connection between the theory (arbitrarily high bit-rate) and the empirical setting is left largely qualitative.

As a paper advancing an actual data-exfiltration attack method, the ethical framing is fairly brief; more detail on the responsible disclosure process or concrete mitigation guidance beyond the proposed (white-box-only) detection method would strengthen the ethics treatment given the described threat model explicitly targets institutions handling sensitive data.

strengths: Formalizes payload recoverability along two well-motivated axes (tokens→buckets and buckets→secret) using classifier-accuracy proxies, providing a concrete, measurable notion that improves on prior informal treatments of steganographic 'stealthiness'.

The proposed embedding-geometry-based encoding/bucketing scheme is a natural and elegant idea (leveraging learned representation structure rather than arbitrary ASCII/parity rules), and it is shown to simultaneously reduce measured recoverability while improving exact-match accuracy across three different base models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B) and multiple fine-tuning regimes (LoRA/full).

Provides theoretical lower bounds (Theorems 7.1, 7.2) showing that substantial payloads can be hidden while KL divergence and perplexity remain within typical fine-tuning noise, giving principled justification for why standard steganalysis is insufficient against this class of attack.

The mechanistic-interpretability detection approach (linear probes on late-layer activations) is a genuinely novel angle for this threat model, and the secret-conditioned XOR-masking control is a clever way to decouple output-level non-decodability from internal detectability, strengthening the causal claim that fine-tuning leaves internal traces independent of output recoverability.

Broad and fairly rigorous experimental scope: OOD prompt-style generalization, text-quality metrics, downstream capability benchmarks (MMLU/ARC/HellaSwag/Winogrande), mixed-motive training to test deployability, and robustness checks (decoding temperature, tokenizer retokenization flip rates) included in appendices, which aids reproducibility and situates the attack more realistically.

Reasonably thorough and honest limitations section (threat-model assumptions, hyperplane-search scalability, output-only detection gap, symbolic-task degradation) rather than glossing over shortcomings.
weaknesses: Despite improvements, absolute exact-match rates remain modest (roughly 17-48%), and several configurations show no gain or even regressions (e.g., Embedding+Embedding on TrojanStego data, ASCII+Embedding on Wiki for Ministral Full), making the practical severity of the 'improved' attack somewhat overstated relative to the reported relative percentage gains.

The recoverability metric is defined as a max over a specific, finite set of classifier families (XGBoost, MLP); this is an empirical upper-bound proxy rather than a principled information-theoretic guarantee, and an adaptive analyst using different features (e.g., a probe trained directly to search for hyperplane structure) might recover more than reported, which is not explored.

Residual Rbucket values for the proposed embedding scheme are still well above chance (~0.6-0.7 rather than ~0.5), so the claim of an 'unrecoverable' or near-random encoding is only partially supported; the paper could more clearly delineate how much recoverability reduction is actually achieved versus merely reduced from perfect.

Capability degradation from steganographic fine-tuning is severe (up to 30+ points on standard benchmarks) and only partially mitigated by mixed-motive training (worse for full fine-tuning), raising doubts about whether the attack is practically deployable as claimed—this tension is acknowledged but not fully resolved.

Detection results are inconsistent across settings (e.g., unclear separation for Ministral-8B full fine-tuning, and bit-accuracy detection under XOR-masking succeeds in only 3 of 8 tested scenarios), which somewhat undercuts the strength of the headline detection claims.

The detection method fundamentally requires white-box access to hidden states, limiting its applicability to the more realistic black-box/API deployment scenarios that motivate the threat model in the first place; this is acknowledged only briefly as future work.

The paper covers a very large number of sub-contributions (recoverability metric, new encoding scheme, KL/PPL bounds, capability benchmarking, mixed-motive training, probe-based detection, XOR-masking control, retokenization robustness) which, combined with dense tables and abbreviations, makes the presentation difficult to follow and dilutes focus; a more streamlined narrative or additional summarization of key trends would improve clarity.
